title: THE WOMAN EVERYONE CALLED A SINNER… AND THE FEET JESUS REFUSED TO PULL AWAY
paragraphs: THE WOMAN EVERYONE CALLED A SINNER… AND THE FEET JESUS REFUSED TO PULL AWAY

She walked into a room where nobody wanted her, carrying a past everybody remembered. But when her tears touched the feet of Jesus, something happened that exposed the hearts of the religious, shattered the power of shame, and revealed a Savior who sees what the world refuses to see.
There is something deeply unsettling about this story.
A woman entered a house where she was not welcome.
She was known for her sins. Her reputation had apparently arrived long before she did. The people in that room did not need an introduction. They already had an opinion.
And she knew it.
Imagine walking into a room where people know the worst things about your life.
Not your kindness. Not your private battles. Not the nights you cried because you hated what you had become.
Only your failures.
Imagine knowing that every glance might be another accusation.
Every whisper might be another reminder.
Every uncomfortable silence might be another judgment.
Now imagine walking into that room anyway.
Not because you had finally become respectable.
Not because you had convinced everyone you had changed.
But because Jesus was there.
And somehow, being near Him mattered more than being humiliated by everyone else.
That is where this story begins.
But what happened next reveals something far greater than a woman crying at the feet of Christ.
It reveals the terrifying possibility that a person can sit at the same table as Jesus, know religious language, maintain a respectable reputation, and still completely misunderstand His heart.
And it reveals something equally astonishing.
The person everyone considered spiritually unworthy might be the one who understands grace most deeply.
In Luke 7:36–50, Jesus accepted an invitation to eat at the home of a Pharisee named Simon.
Simon belonged to a religious movement known for its concern with obedience to God's law and traditions of religious purity.
He had invited Jesus into his home.
There would have been food, conversation, and the social expectations surrounding a meal in that culture.
Then something unexpected happened.
Luke writes:
— Luke 7:37, KJV
Notice what Scripture does not tell us.
It does not give her name.
It does not identify the specific sins for which she was known.
It does not say she was a prostitute, although that assumption has frequently appeared in retellings of this passage.
It does not identify her as Mary Magdalene.
And it does not identify her as Mary of Bethany, whose anointing of Jesus is recorded in another setting.
Luke simply calls her a woman who was known as a sinner.
That description was enough for Simon.
But it was not the whole story for Jesus.
Because people often remember the chapter of your life you are most desperate to leave behind.
They remember what you did.
They remember who you were.
They remember the scandal.
But they cannot always see what God is doing inside you now.
And perhaps that is why this story still hurts.
Because somewhere, someone reading this has spent years trying to escape a reputation that other people refuse to let die.
Maybe it was an affair.
Maybe an addiction.
Maybe a betrayal.
Maybe years of hypocrisy, secret compromises, or decisions that damaged people you genuinely loved.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
And perhaps the most exhausting part is not what others remember.
It is what you cannot seem to forgive yourself for.
You have asked God for mercy, but the memory still returns.
You have tried to move forward, but shame keeps dragging yesterday into today.
You have smiled in church while silently wondering whether the people sitting beside you would still embrace you if they knew everything.
And beneath all those thoughts lies one question you are almost afraid to ask.
Would Jesus still let someone like me come close?
The woman in Luke 7 gives us a remarkable picture of the answer.
She approached Jesus from behind as He reclined at the table.
Then the tears began.
Luke 7:38 says:
"And stood at his feet behind him weeping, and began to wash his feet with tears, and did wipe them with the hairs of her head, and kissed his feet, and anointed them with the ointment."
Read that slowly.
She did not arrive with a prepared speech recorded for us.
She did not stand before the guests and explain her circumstances.
She did not attempt to defend her reputation.
She wept.
And the tears fell upon the feet of Jesus.
In the Greek text, Luke uses the word βρέχειν (brechein), meaning to wet or moisten, describing what her tears did to His feet.
The picture is intimate and deeply human.
Her tears were so abundant that they wet His feet.
She then wiped them with her hair, kissed them repeatedly, and anointed them with perfume.
The Greek verb κατεφίλει (katephilei) conveys affectionate kissing, and its form in this passage presents the action as continuing.
This was not a quick ceremonial gesture.
It was an extraordinary expression of love and humility.
And Jesus allowed it.
He did not pull His feet away.
He did not publicly shame her.
He did not demand that she first explain herself to the people watching.
He did not tell her that her reputation made her unfit to approach Him.
He received her act of devotion.
But we must understand something important.
Jesus was not approving her sins.
He was receiving a repentant sinner.
There is a world of difference.
The Gospel never teaches that sin is harmless.
Sin separates us from the holiness of God. It corrupts our desires, wounds relationships, and leads toward death.
Romans 6:23 declares that the wages of sin is death.
Jesus did not come to convince sinners that repentance was unnecessary.
He came to save sinners.
And salvation is far greater than being told that our wrongdoing does not matter.
It means that the Son of God takes sin so seriously that He willingly goes to the cross to deal with it.
Grace is not God pretending that evil is good.
Grace is God providing redemption for the guilty through Jesus Christ.
And the woman at His feet was about to discover how publicly and personally Jesus would speak of forgiveness.
But before Jesus addressed her, another heart was being exposed.
Simon was watching.
And what he thought reveals the danger of religious pride.
Luke 7:39 records his private judgment:
"This man, if he were a prophet, would have known who and what manner of woman this is that toucheth him: for she is a sinner."
Simon thought he understood the situation.
He saw a sinful woman touching a religious teacher.
And he concluded that Jesus must lack spiritual discernment.
Surely, Simon reasoned, a true prophet would know what kind of woman this was.
But here is the extraordinary irony.
Jesus knew.
He knew enough to recognize the woman's condition.
And He also knew what Simon was thinking.
The Pharisee believed Jesus was failing to recognize sin.
In reality, Simon was failing to recognize mercy.
One man saw a scandal.
Jesus saw a woman whose love revealed a heart responding to grace.
And the Savior was about to show Simon that his greatest problem was not the woman standing near the table.
It was the pride sitting comfortably inside his own heart.
Jesus turned toward Simon and said that He had something to tell him.
Then He described two debtors.
One owed five hundred denarii.
The other owed fifty.
A denarius was commonly associated with a day's wage for a laborer, making both debts significant, although one was ten times larger than the other.
Neither debtor could repay what he owed.
That detail matters.
The smaller debtor was not capable of saving himself simply because his debt was smaller.
Both were helpless before the creditor.
Then the creditor freely forgave both debts.
Jesus asked Simon which debtor would love the creditor more.
Simon answered that it would be the one forgiven more.
Jesus affirmed his answer.
And suddenly the story was no longer merely about money.
It was about forgiveness.
About love.
About the human tendency to measure ourselves against other sinners instead of recognizing our own need for mercy.
The Greek verb used for the creditor's gracious cancellation of the debts is ἐχαρίσατο (echarisato), from χαρίζομαι (charizomai), a verb associated with freely giving or graciously granting.
The debtors did not purchase their release.
They received it.
That is essential to understanding what happened at Jesus' feet.
The woman was not buying forgiveness with perfume.
She was not purchasing salvation through tears.
She was not earning God's acceptance by demonstrating enough emotion.
Her love was evidence of her response to grace, not the price she paid for it.
Jesus then turned toward the woman while continuing to speak to Simon.
And what He said must have made that room profoundly uncomfortable.
"Seest thou this woman?"
— Luke 7:44, KJV
What a question.
Simon had been looking at her the entire time.
But Jesus asked whether he actually saw her.
Because there is a difference between looking at someone and seeing them.
Simon saw her reputation.
Jesus drew attention to her devotion.
Simon saw a category.
Jesus saw a person.
Simon saw the sin associated with her past.
Jesus recognized the love being expressed before Him.
And perhaps that question should disturb us more than we want to admit.
Do you see this woman?
Do you see the single mother whose history has become church gossip?
Do you see the young man struggling with pornography who is terrified to ask for help?
Do you see the former addict who fears that one mistake will convince everyone that he has never changed?
Do you see the believer who fell into sin, repented, and now wonders whether there is still a place for them among God's people?
Do you see the person who has hurt others and must still take responsibility, but desperately needs to know that repentance and restoration are possible?
Or do you only see what they did?
This is not a call to ignore wrongdoing, silence victims, or remove accountability.
Biblical mercy does not erase the need for truth, justice, restitution, or changed behavior.
But neither does biblical holiness authorize us to treat repentant sinners as permanently beyond the reach of God's grace.
Jesus never confused compassion with moral compromise.
And He never needed cruelty to demonstrate holiness.
Then He confronted Simon with three failures of hospitality.
Simon had provided no water for Jesus' feet.
The woman had wet His feet with her tears and wiped them with her hair.
Simon had given Him no kiss of greeting.
The woman had continued kissing His feet.
Simon had not anointed His head with oil.
The woman had anointed His feet with perfume.
These gestures carried meaning in the social world of the passage, although not every omission necessarily constituted a formal violation of hospitality.
Jesus' point was unmistakable.
The woman whom Simon despised had demonstrated an extraordinary love that Simon himself had failed to show.
Simon had welcomed Jesus into his house.
But the woman had approached Him with a heart overflowing in devotion.
And here lies a warning that every Christian, including the person writing these words, needs to hear.
It is possible to become familiar with religious activity while losing our tenderness toward Christ.
We can learn the vocabulary of grace without being humbled by it.
We can defend biblical truth while forgetting that the truth reveals our own desperate need for a Savior.
We can recognize sin in someone else's life while quietly excusing the pride, bitterness, envy, and lovelessness growing inside our own.
We can attend worship and still withhold our hearts.
We can become more concerned with looking righteous than with being reconciled to God.
Simon was close enough to Jesus to share a meal.
Yet he was in danger of missing the significance of the mercy unfolding before his eyes.
The woman had no impressive religious standing in the narrative.
Yet her actions displayed a love that Jesus publicly acknowledged.
Then came one of the most important statements in the entire account.
Jesus said:
"Wherefore I say unto thee, Her sins, which are many, are forgiven; for she loved much: but to whom little is forgiven, the same loveth little."
— Luke 7:47, KJV
This verse must be read carefully.
At first glance, someone might assume Jesus meant that her love earned forgiveness.
But the parable immediately preceding it establishes the opposite order.
The creditor forgave the debts, and that forgiveness produced love.
The woman's extraordinary love demonstrated the reality of forgiveness, rather than purchasing it.
The Greek word ἀφέωνται (apheōntai), translated "are forgiven," is a perfect passive form of ἀφίημι (aphiēmi).
It presents her sins as having been forgiven, with the resulting state continuing.
Jesus was not teaching that enough tears can remove guilt.
He was revealing the gracious forgiveness that lay behind her love.
This is why we must resist turning her story into a message that says, "Cry hard enough, worship passionately enough, give enough money, and God will finally accept you."
That is not the Gospel.
The Gospel is that sinners who cannot rescue themselves are called to repent and believe in Jesus Christ, whose death and resurrection provide the foundation of forgiveness and new life.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast."
The woman did not save herself by washing Jesus' feet.
Her tears were not a second Savior.
Her perfume was not a substitute for the cross.
And her public humiliation was not payment for her sins.
Jesus Christ alone saves.
Her actions expressed the love of someone who recognized how much mercy she needed.
And this changes the way we read the entire encounter.
Because the greatest miracle in that room was not that Jesus tolerated an embarrassing interruption.
It was that the Holy One of God could receive a sinner without becoming sinful Himself.
The religious instinct of Simon's judgment was to create distance from someone he regarded as morally contaminated.
But Jesus was not made unholy by the woman's touch.
His holiness was not fragile.
His mercy was not weakness.
His authority was not threatened by her past.
He was the Savior who came to seek and save the lost.
And the road that would eventually lead Him to Calvary was already revealing the depth of His mission.
Think about it.
The woman brought perfume.
Jesus would ultimately give His life.
The woman came carrying the shame of her sins.
Jesus would bear sin's judgment in His saving work upon the cross.
The woman knelt at His feet.
And those feet would one day be pierced in the crucifixion.
Luke does not explicitly connect these particular details in this scene, so we should not pretend they are hidden predictions.
But as we read this encounter in the light of the completed Gospel, the contrast is overwhelming.
She brought what she could.
Christ would accomplish what she never could.
She could express love.
Only He could provide salvation.
And that is why this story is not ultimately about the greatness of a woman's tears.
It is about the greatness of the Savior who received her.
There is another detail we cannot overlook.
Jesus did not merely defend her before Simon.
He spoke directly to her.
"And he said unto her, Thy sins are forgiven."
— Luke 7:48, KJV
Imagine what those words meant.
For a woman whose public identity was bound to sin, Jesus spoke a declaration of forgiveness.
The people at the table began asking among themselves who this man was who even forgave sins.
Their question was theologically significant.
In Scripture, forgiveness of sins ultimately belongs to God.
Jesus was exercising an authority that demanded an answer about His identity.
He was not merely offering emotional reassurance.
He was speaking with divine authority.
And then came the final words recorded to the woman.
"Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace."
— Luke 7:50, KJV
Not, "Your perfume has saved you."
Not, "Your tears have saved you."
Not, "Your public display has saved you."
Your faith has saved you.
The Greek reads:
Ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε· πορεύου εἰς εἰρήνην.
Hē pistis sou sesōken se; poreuou eis eirēnēn.
"Your faith has saved you; go in peace."
The verb σέσωκέν (sesōken), from σῴζω (sōzō), is a perfect active form meaning "has saved," emphasizing a saving action with an enduring result.
And the final word, εἰρήνη (eirēnē), means peace.
This is more than a casual goodbye.
In the context of Jesus' declaration of forgiveness and salvation, it is a beautiful dismissal into the peace associated with God's saving mercy.
She entered a room where her sin was publicly remembered.
She left having heard Jesus declare forgiveness and salvation.
Luke does not tell us what happened to her afterward.
We do not know where she went, what conversations followed, or how her life unfolded.
Scripture leaves those details unwritten.
And perhaps that restraint is important.
We do not need to invent a dramatic future for her to recognize the extraordinary grace of what Jesus actually said.
Her story is already powerful enough.
But now the question turns toward us.
What if the thing keeping you away from Jesus is the very thing you most urgently need to bring before Him?
What if you have mistaken shame for repentance?
What if you believe that hating yourself is somehow proof that you are becoming holy?
What if you have spent years punishing yourself for sins that you should be confessing to God and turning away from in faith?
There is a difference between godly sorrow and hopeless condemnation.
Second Corinthians 7:10 teaches that godly sorrow produces repentance leading to salvation, while worldly sorrow produces death.
True repentance does not merely say, "I feel terrible about what I did."
It turns toward God.
It acknowledges sin without excuses.
It seeks mercy through Christ.
And where our actions have harmed others, it bears fruit through changed conduct, responsibility, and appropriate efforts to make things right.
Repentance is not pretending the past never happened.
It is refusing to let the past remain your master.
And faith is not confidence that you have finally become good enough.
It is trust in the Savior who is sufficient.
Perhaps you have been waiting to feel clean before approaching Jesus.
But sinners do not make themselves clean and then earn the right to come to Him.
They come to Him for cleansing.
First John 1:9 declares:
"If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Notice that Scripture does not say God forgives because we have successfully hidden the evidence.
It calls us to confession.
To truth.
To the light.
And to the mercy of God.
This does not mean that forgiveness eliminates every earthly consequence.
A broken marriage may require years of rebuilding trust.
A damaged relationship may not be restored immediately.
A criminal act may still carry legal consequences.
A person who has been harmed is not obligated to abandon wise boundaries simply because an offender says they have repented.
But none of those realities cancels the promise that genuine forgiveness and transformation are available through Jesus Christ.
Grace is not permission to continue destroying your life.
Grace is the beginning of a new way of living.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains believers to reject ungodliness and worldly desires and to live godly lives.
The same grace that welcomes sinners also teaches them to leave sin behind.
That is why our message at Gospel Warrior is not that your past was harmless.
It is that your past does not have to have the final word.
Not by rewriting history.
Not by calling evil good.
Not by removing the need for repentance.
But by redeeming sinners, giving new life, and transforming those who belong to Him.
Second Corinthians 5:17 declares that anyone in Christ is a new creature.
That is not a motivational slogan.
It is a declaration of what God's saving work makes possible.
And perhaps someone needs to hear this today.
You are not beyond the reach of Christ because people know your worst chapter.
You are not too stained to repent.
You are not too far away to call upon His name.
You are not disqualified from seeking mercy because you once lived in rebellion.
But do not confuse the availability of grace with a guarantee that tomorrow will be yours.
The call of the Gospel is urgent.
Turn to Christ.
Not when you have successfully repaired your reputation.
Not when everybody has forgiven you.
Not when you can finally speak about your past without crying.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Today.
Because the same Jesus who received the woman in Simon's house is the risen Lord who calls sinners to Himself.
And He is worthy of more than our admiration.
He is worthy of our trust, worship, obedience, and entire lives.
If this story has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to publish the details of your sin for strangers to examine.
But you can take a small, sincere step toward the light.
And if you have experienced the forgiveness of Christ, consider sharing a brief testimony. Your words may encourage someone who believes their life is already beyond redemption.
You never know who is silently reading.
The person who looks confident online may be carrying unbearable guilt.
The friend who never misses church may be struggling with secret sin.
The family member who seems distant from God may be longing for a reason to believe that forgiveness is still possible.
That is why sharing this message matters.
Not merely to increase the reach of a page, but because the truth of Christ deserves to be heard beyond the walls of our familiar circles.
We also want to speak openly about something important.
Producing and sharing Christ-centered teaching requires time, effort, resources, and continued support.
Our desire is to keep reaching people who are searching for truth, believers who need strengthening, and wounded hearts that need to hear the message of Jesus Christ.
It can be part of your personal Christian generosity and stewardship, offered with a grateful heart before God.
But we want to be clear about something Scripture makes essential.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
Not a promise that money can purchase spiritual reward.
But willing partnership in a mission that seeks to make Christ known.
These products are simply additional resources and expressions of encouragement. They are not measures of spiritual maturity, and purchasing them is never a requirement for discipleship.
Your prayers matter.
Your encouragement matters.
Your willingness to share sound biblical teaching matters.
There is also a growing resource available to help you continue studying Scripture.
These resources are intended to help believers grow in biblical understanding, strengthen their prayer lives, develop spiritual discernment, and deepen their walk with Jesus Christ.
Because the ultimate goal of this ministry is not to make people dependent on a Facebook page.
It is to point them toward Jesus Christ, His Word, and faithful life within His Church.
Because the woman in Luke 7 did not encounter a Savior who needed her perfume.
She encountered a Savior whose grace she desperately needed.
And that is where we must return before this story ends.
To the room.
To the table.
To Simon.
To the woman.
To Jesus.
Picture that final moment.
The religious guests were questioning His authority to forgive sins.
The woman had heard the words that mattered most.
"Thy faith hath saved thee; go in peace."
We do not know whether she walked out still crying.
We do not know whether Simon's opinion changed.
We do not know whether the other guests treated her differently afterward.
But we know what Jesus said.
And that is enough.
Because the final authority over her standing before God did not belong to Simon.
It belonged to Christ.
And the same truth confronts us today.
People may remember your scandal.
Some may never understand your repentance.
Others may refuse to believe that you have changed.
And when you have harmed someone, their pain deserves to be taken seriously, even as you seek to walk in newness of life.
But no human reputation can replace the judgment of God.
And no human approval can accomplish the salvation that only Jesus gives.
So stop trying to purchase peace through endless self-punishment.
Stop mistaking religious appearance for a surrendered heart.
Stop believing that hiding your sin will somehow heal it.
Bring your guilt to Christ.
Confess what is true.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Trust the One who died for sinners and rose again.
And learn to walk in the peace that His Gospel provides.
The woman came to Jesus with tears.
But the deepest truth of the story is not that she cried.
It is that Jesus forgave.
That is the hope of the Gospel.
That is the beauty of grace.
And that is why no scandal is greater than the saving power of Jesus Christ.
The world may keep calling you by the name of your worst mistake, but when Christ forgives you, your sin no longer has the authority to write the ending of your story.
